title: Primal supernova seeds the solar nebula

facts.text: A supernova shock wave in a dense part of the Milky Way seeded the region with heavy elements later built into Earth.
Calcium–aluminium-rich inclusions, which formed 2 million years before chondrules, are a key signature of this supernova.
Its shock wave may have triggered the solar nebula's collapse and set it rotating.

title: Birth of the Sun and Solar System
article: Formation and evolution of the Solar System

facts.text: The Sun formed from the rapid collapse of a hydrogen molecular cloud, about 25,000 light years from the center of the Milky Way.
The spinning cloud flattened into a protoplanetary disc, the raw material of Earth, around the young T Tauri Sun.
Calcium–aluminium-rich inclusions, the first solids to condense from the hot disc, date to 4,567.30 ± 0.16 Ma; this age defines the Solar System's start and the Hadean's.
The young Sun's solar wind cleared out most disc material not yet gathered into larger bodies; by 10 million years the disc's gas was gone.
The Sun has grown about 30% brighter since it formed.

title: Iron catastrophe: Earth's core forms

facts.text: In a geologically brief, postulated event, the iron catastrophe, dense iron and nickel sank to the centre of the young Earth to form its core.
Radioactive heating and leftover accretion heat melted the planet enough for metal to move; the sinking metal released energy in a runaway process.
Timing is uncertain: hafnium–tungsten models give 30–100 million years after the first solids, depending on giant-impact mixing; other sources say 10 or about 500 million years in.
It separated a metallic core, where siderophile metals gathered, from a primitive mantle, giving Earth its layered structure of core, mantle and crust.
The spinning molten metal set up Earth's magnetic field, which still shields the atmosphere and life from the solar wind.

title: Possible onset of plate tectonics

facts.text: Radiogenic heat and water still in the mantle lowered its viscosity, so Hadean mantle convection was vigorous.
Whether this convection drove plate tectonics or stayed trapped under a rigid lid is still debated.
Hadean oceans are thought to have triggered plate tectonics; one view has it starting vigorously, then slowing in the Archean.
Removal of the CO2-rich early atmosphere, helped by subduction of carbonate, is cited as evidence for Hadean plate tectonics.
Zircon evidence comes almost entirely from one Australian locality, and some geologists think those zircons formed in impacts.

facts.text: In runaway accretion, dust and debris from the solar nebula clumped into ever larger bodies, building Earth.
The proto-Earth formed at the cool outer edge of the habitable zone and grew through a series of giant impacts.
Accretion was largely complete within 10–20 million years, though one estimate allows 70–100 million and 2023 evidence suggests only about three million.
Accretion began soon after the first solids formed; Earth's age, 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years, marks the final stages of accretion and differentiation.
Shortly after it formed, Earth spun fast: a day lasted only about six hours.

title: Global magma ocean covers Earth

facts.text: A magma ocean about 200 km deep covered Earth, melted by the Moon-forming and other impacts and by heat from forming the core.
Earth probably had a series of magma oceans from giant impacts; the last, from the Moon-forming impact, may have reached 2,000 km deep.
Siderophile elements in the mantle record magma-ocean depths of about 1,000 km during accretion.
The initial magma ocean solidified within about 5 million years, leaving hot volatiles that formed a heavy CO2 atmosphere.
Evidence is weaker than for the Moon, because Earth's crust is recycled and its mantle mixed.

contested_note: Sources disagree: the Magma ocean page cites chemical evidence, but the Giant-impact hypothesis page says there is no evidence Earth ever had one.

title: Faint young Sun kept warm by greenhouse

facts.text: The young Sun gave only about 70% of today's output, so early Earth should have frozen, yet it seems to have had liquid water and life.
Models find that at 4.5 Ga, under a 30% dimmer Sun, at least 0.1 bar of CO2 was needed to stay above freezing; 10 bar is a plausible upper limit.
Greenhouse gases are thought to have kept the oceans from freezing; the carbonate–silicate cycle lets CO2 build up when cold slows weathering.
The Sun became a main-sequence star about 4.5 Ga and has brightened since; it now shines 1.4 times as bright as 4.6 Ga.
How much CO2 there was is still debated; other proposed answers include a lower surface albedo and mass loss from the young Sun.

sources.title: Formation and evolution of the Solar System

contested_note: How early Earth stayed warm under the dim Sun is an unsolved problem, and the amount of CO2 is still debated.

facts.text: A Mars-sized protoplanet, Theia, struck the proto-Earth about 20–100 million years after the Solar System formed.
Debris thrown into orbit lingered as rings for a few million years, then gathered into the Moon.
The impact probably vaporized much of Earth's crust and upper mantle, wrapping the planet in rock vapor and disrupting any earlier water.
It is the favored explanation of the Moon's origin among astronomers; lunar rocks date the Moon to 4.53 ± 0.01 billion years.
The Moon's pull steadied Earth's wobbling axis of rotation, making climate more regular.

facts.text: About 100 million years after the Moon formed, its first crust, made of anorthosite, separated out from the magma below.
This ferroan anorthosite is read as plagioclase crystals that floated up through the lunar magma ocean, which was at first 200–300 km thick.
Anorthosite makes the pale lunar highlands, about 80% of the Moon's surface; ferroan anorthosites are dated to about 4.4 Ga.

facts.text: Zircon crystals show that liquid water and an atmosphere existed by 4.404 ± 0.008 Ga, very soon after Earth formed.
As the crust and surface cooled, water vapor condensed into a superocean covering nearly the whole planet.
The oceans stayed liquid despite the heat because the air pressure was about 27 atmospheres.
The water most likely came from mantle outgassing; isotopes make comets an unlikely main source.
Earth may have been mostly a water world between 4.4 and 4.3 Ga; dissolved CO2 probably made the seas slightly acidic, about pH 5.5.

title: Oldest known mineral: Jack Hills zircon

facts.text: The oldest dated mineral on Earth is a zircon crystal from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, 4.404 ± 0.008 Ga old.
It lies in a metamorphosed conglomerate of the Narryer Gneiss terrane; most zircons there are only 3.6–3.8 Ga old.
The 4.404 Ga grain is a slight outlier; the oldest consistently dated zircons are closer to 4.35 Ga.
Hadean zircons crystallized at fairly low temperatures from evolved melts and carry heavy oxygen, hinting at crust-forming processes like today's.
Hadean zircon is rare worldwide because plate tectonics recycled the crust that held it.

verification.title: Evidence from detrital zircons for the existence of continental crust and oceans on the Earth 4.4 Gyr ago

facts.text: Early Hadean Earth first had a very thick, hydride-rich atmosphere like the solar nebula; the Moon-forming impact stripped this primary atmosphere away.
The cooling magma ocean released carbon dioxide and water, giving a heavy CO2 atmosphere at about 230 °C and over 27 atmospheres.
Outgassing from the crust had built this secondary atmosphere by 4,404 Ma at the latest, a minimum age.
Comets and carbonaceous chondrites added water and possibly organic molecules.
Volcanic outgassing and impacts later turned it into the nitrogen- and CO2-rich, weakly reducing atmosphere of the Paleoarchean.
Zircons formed 4.4 Ga show the crust solidified about 100 million years after Earth formed; one source puts a stable crust in place by 4,433 Ma.
The first crust, formed as Earth's molten outer layer cooled, was probably mafic; partial melting of it made the first, more felsic continental crust.
The earliest crust probably formed like the Moon's first crust, from similar materials separating out of the magma.
Hafnium isotopes in zircons fit crust forming from 4.5 Ga onward, possibly an early reservoir like continental crust.
Only mineral grains survive from the Hadean crust; the oldest whole rock formations at the surface are Archean.

title: Cool early Earth

facts.text: The cool early Earth hypothesis holds that temperatures were cold enough to freeze water between about 4.4 and 4.0 Ga.
The source calls this somewhat of a paradox, since zircons show liquid water by 4.404 Ga.
The Precambrian page allows a possible cool period within the bombardment-dominated Hadean.

contested_note: A hypothesis that the source sets against zircon evidence for liquid water, calling the clash a paradox.

facts.text: Impacts declined; the last one big enough to vaporize the oceans struck about 4.3 Ga, and life probably emerged after it.
Later Hadean impacts were thousands to millions of years apart, but life stayed vulnerable to large ones.
Before about 4.3–4.2 Ga, Earth was very hostile to life.

title: Possible microfossils at Nuvvuagittuq

facts.text: Possible fossil microorganisms occur in hydrothermal-vent deposits from an ancient seabed in Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq Belt, dated 3.77 to 4.28 Ga.
If 4.28 Ga old, they would be the oldest record of life, suggesting it emerged almost at once, in geological terms, after the oceans formed.
Silica-rich waters, chemical gardens, hydrothermal fluids and volcanic ejecta can mimic such shapes, so the traces may not be biological.

contested_note: Disputed: the structures may have formed without life, and the host rocks' age is itself contested.

title: Light carbon in 4.25 Ga Jack Hills zircons

facts.text: Jack Hills zircons in Western Australia hold unusually light carbon isotopes, a common sign of life.
The carbon is trapped in tiny pieces of diamond and graphite inside zircons dated to 4.25 Ga.
Studies in 2005, 2006 and 2009 found no light carbon of the kind behind earlier claims of Hadean life.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether the light carbon is there at all, and a biological origin is unproven.

title: Hadean zircons in Guyana's Iwokrama Formation

facts.text: Zircon cores from the Iwokrama Formation of southern Guyana, in the Guiana Shield, have been dated to 4.22 Ga by U–Pb laser-ablation analysis.
Hadean zircons inside younger rocks show those rocks formed on older terranes and took in some of the older material.
Eastern Brazil has also yielded 4.22 Ga material of felsic magmatic origin, rich in uranium.

verification.title: Guyana: the Lost Hadean crust of South America?

title: Hadean granite crust beneath Acasta Gneiss

facts.text: The Acasta rocks of Canada's Slave Craton grew partly from Hadean protocrust; zircon xenocrysts in their 3.94 Ga gneisses give U–Pb dates of 4.2 Ga.
The gneisses partly derive from this 4.2 Ga granite magma, showing that early crust was melted and reworked.
Zircons from the granite resemble Western Australia's Yilgarn zircons and may record Hadean continental crust.

title: Last universal common ancestor (LUCA)

facts.text: A 2024 molecular-clock study put LUCA, ancestor of all living things, at about 4.2 Ga (range 4.33–4.09 Ga): a genetic estimate, not a fossil.
That implies only about 100–200 million years between life's origin and LUCA, as the first habitable environments likely formed around 4.3–4.4 Ga.
A 2018 molecular-clock study concluded LUCA predated the Late Heavy Bombardment, making it over 3.9 Ga.
Other estimates run from 4.52–4.48 Ga (2018) to 4.2–3.6 Ga (2022) and 3.8–3.5 Ga (2000-era); most agree it existed by 3.5 Ga.

contested_note: This is a genetic estimate, not a fossil; other studies range from 4.5 to 3.5 billion years.

title: Growth of the first continental crust

facts.text: Models disagree on how much continental crust the Hadean had; in some, a global ocean covered Earth.
Models by Korenaga and colleagues have continental crust reaching today's volume between 4.2 and 4.0 Ga.
Dhuime and colleagues instead estimate only 25% of today's continental area by the end of the Hadean.
Continents may have appeared in the mid-Hadean, then vanished beneath a thick ocean by the eon's end.
Small proto-continents are generally thought to have existed before 4,280 Ma.

contested_note: Hadean continent growth rests on disputed models of early tectonics; estimates run from a quarter of today's area to today's full volume.

title: Nuvvuagittuq rocks, possibly Earth's oldest

facts.text: A gabbro dike cutting the belt's Ujaraaluk unit dates to 4,157 Ma, a minimum age showing its mafic rocks are Hadean.
Samarium–neodymium dating in 2012 gave the Quebec belt 4,321 Ma, which would make it Earth's oldest known rock.
Other studies accept only a minimum of 3.75 Ga and argue the 4,321 Ma signal was inherited from older, melted Hadean crust.

contested_note: Its age is debated: at least 3.75 billion years, and possibly over 4.1 billion.

title: Origin of life (abiogenesis)

facts.text: Abundant Hadean geothermal settings, possibly including hot springs on volcanic land, may have let RNA form and copy itself, a possible route to life.
Evidence suggests the first RNA molecules formed before 4.17 Ga.
Geochemical evidence puts life's origin possibly as early as 4.1 Ga; some models and researchers propose nearly 4.5 Ga.
Life may have begun as far back as 4.4 Ga in hydrothermal vents, shielded from impacts and ultraviolet light; a deep-vent origin would allow 4.0–4.2 Ga.
The geologic record puts life's emergence most likely between 4.32 and 3.48 Ga; some sources call Hadean evidence of life controversial.

contested_note: When life began is unknown, and the sources call evidence of Hadean life controversial.

facts.text: Carbon in 4.1-billion-year-old zircon from Western Australia may be remains of life.
Such carbon-isotope anomalies are chemical fossils and could be the oldest traces of life on Earth.
The evidence is preliminary and still needs confirmation.

contested_note: The carbon may not be biological; the claim is preliminary, and claims of the earliest life are contested.

title: Late Heavy Bombardment

facts.text: Crater counts suggest intense impacts from about 4.1 to 3.8 Ga, cratering the Moon and, by inference, Earth, Mercury, Venus and Mars.
The main evidence is a clustering of Apollo impact-melt ages between about 3.8 and 4.1 Ga, from samples mostly near the Imbrium Basin.
Once widely accepted, it is now debated: critics see the cluster as debris of one large impact, and some evidence favors bombardment from 4.2 to 3.5 Ga.
It may have been caused by Neptune migrating outward through orbital resonances between Jupiter and Saturn.
Life either arose afterward or, more likely, survived it; hydrothermal heat may even have helped life begin.

contested_note: Scientists still argue whether there was a distinct late spike in impacts or a long, gradual decline.
